items.title: Continuous accountability for Verified bots
items.summary: A driver’s license tells you who someone is and that they passed a driving test, not whether they’ll drive responsibly in the future. The same is true for bots: verifying who operates it creates accountability, but trust depends on what it does next. A known bot can still ignore website preferences, overwhelm origins, or evade controls. It’s not always malicious — often it’s just a misconfiguration or a bug. As we described in a previous blog post on bot behavior, we strive to verify two questions: “Are you who you say you are?” and “Can we trust you?” To be a Cloudflare Verified Bot, you broadly need to meet three criteria: Identify yourself accurately and securely Do only what you say you will do Don’t engage in abusive behavior Bots use Web Bot Auth to sign requests that establish their identity, which BotBase then catalogues in an open format. With identification addressed, our focus shifts to the second cardinal rule of Verified bots: thou shalt do no harm . Today we introduce a system to evaluate and report when Verified bot behavior starts to deviate from this rule, ensuring that the answer to “Can we trust you?” remains “Yes.” This is where the distinction between risk and trust becomes important: Risk describes the likelihood that a particular request or point-in-time action may be harmful, and it can change from one moment to the next. Trust is built over time through repeated and consistent behavior. For example, we de-listed Perplexity’s bot from our Verified bot list in 2025 when it sought to access resources on websites that opted out of scraping and subsequently attempted to circumvent controls when those requests were blocked. Do not engage in abusive behavior This simple requirement sounds like a freebie, but there is a lot of nuance in that statement. When crawlers don’t respect site preferences , that undermines trust. When sites request a crawler to not crawl or to slow down, and the crawler ignores these requests, that undermines trust. We developed a system to measure how often a crawler respects site preferences. These observations will translate to an explainable trust band: a range showing how consistently a bot respects site preferences and which observed behaviors informed that assessment, rather than a permanent judgment about a bot or its operator. The initial signals we evaluate are: Does the bot respect instructions? Did it respond to direct feedback? We consider these to be “common sense” rules, a courtesy to the operators who provide the information bots seek. In the future, we will be sharing these scores publicly on Radar , as well as expanding the ways we measure. This score gives responsible bot operators a way to demonstrate that trust is being upheld over time. Verify, but continuously re-verify. When in Rome, do as the Romans do A robots.txt file is the primary way to communicate site owner preferences. Our system considers whether a bot’s observed traffic is consistent with those published preferences over time. Robots.txt tells all (or specific) bots to only crawl specific parts of a website. Isolated violations and other types of one-offs may not be significant. What we look for instead are repeated patterns of behavior that disregards site preferences. The expectation is simply for responsible bots to consult and honor the preferences that websites publish, in line with RFC 9309 . And just to be clear, a robots.txt sets the minimum rules for what bots and agents should not do. But there is no implication that anything not stated is allowed. For example, a robots.txt does not need to say that a bot must stop when the site can communicate that continued access is unwelcome through other signals. What you do not wish for yourself, do not impose on others Bots can remain entirely within allowed paths while still placing substantial load on the websites they visit. One of the clearest ways a website can push back is with an HTTP 429 (“Too Many Requests”) response. A 429 is a directive for the visitor to reduce its request rate, sometimes with guidance about how long to wait before trying again. Our system considers whether the bot’s traffic adapts after receiving that signal. Does it slow down, pause, or does it continue sending requests at the same pace? We then incorporate that behavior into the bot’s trust band over time: consistently slowing down or pausing increases trust, while repeatedly ignoring the signal lowers it. Building trust over time Observing these signals is only a first step toward making verified automation accountable over time. By pairing bot identity with evidence of continuing behavior, we can give site owners more confidence that the bots they choose to allow are respecting their preferences, give bot operators a way to demonstrate they deserve trust, and provide context to website owners about the automated traffic reaching them. This system, alongside Bot Preference Sync and Bot Management , forms an accountability loop for automated traffic. Bot Preference Sync helps website owners publish their preferences, and observing how bots interact with these preferences shows whether Verified bots consistently honor them over time. Bot Management lets website owners decide how that traffic is handled. Together, they help ensure that trust is earned through transparent, accountable behavior, not assumed from identity alone. We are already using this system internally to evaluate how consistently Verified bots honor website preferences. Because trust is built over time, we assess sustained patterns rather than isolated events. We are using this initial phase to build that history and refine how those observations become useful guidance. Building on that foundation, we plan to make the system available to all Cloudflare customers, who will be able to choose the trust threshold used to decide how Verified bot traffic is handled. Our goal is straightforward: to keep website preferences meaningful, and ensure trust is earned through sustained behavior. Want to learn more about how you can handle bots? Cloudflare customers can already use Bot Management to manage automated traffic and Bot Preference Sync to align their published preferences with their configured policies. To explore the ever-growing Verified bot population, see the trends on Radar . And if you are interested in helping build the future of bot identity and accountability, explore open roles at Cloudflare .

A driver’s license tells you who someone is and that they passed a driving test, not whether they’ll drive responsibly in the future. The same is true for bots: verifying who operates it creates accountability, but trust depends on what it does next. A known bot can still ignore website preferences, overwhelm origins, or evade controls. It’s not always malicious — often it’s just a misconfiguration or a bug.

As we described in a previous blog post on bot behavior, we strive to verify two questions: “Are you who you say you are?” and “Can we trust you?” To be a Cloudflare Verified Bot, you broadly need to meet three criteria:

  1. Identify yourself accurately and securely
  2. Do only what you say you will do
  3. Don’t engage in abusive behavior

Bots use Web Bot Auth to sign requests that establish their identity, which BotBase then catalogues in an open format. With identification addressed, our focus shifts to the second cardinal rule of Verified bots: thou shalt do no harm.

Today we introduce a system to evaluate and report when Verified bot behavior starts to deviate from this rule, ensuring that the answer to “Can we trust you?” remains “Yes.”

This is where the distinction between risk and trust becomes important:

  • Risk describes the likelihood that a particular request or point-in-time action may be harmful, and it can change from one moment to the next.
  • Trust is built over time through repeated and consistent behavior.

For example, we de-listed Perplexity’s bot from our Verified bot list in 2025 when it sought to access resources on websites that opted out of scraping and subsequently attempted to circumvent controls when those requests were blocked.

Do not engage in abusive behavior

This simple requirement sounds like a freebie, but there is a lot of nuance in that statement. When crawlers don’t respect site preferences, that undermines trust. When sites request a crawler to not crawl or to slow down, and the crawler ignores these requests, that undermines trust.

We developed a system to measure how often a crawler respects site preferences. These observations will translate to an explainable trust band: a range showing how consistently a bot respects site preferences and which observed behaviors informed that assessment, rather than a permanent judgment about a bot or its operator. The initial signals we evaluate are:

  • Does the bot respect instructions?
  • Did it respond to direct feedback?

We consider these to be “common sense” rules, a courtesy to the operators who provide the information bots seek. In the future, we will be sharing these scores publicly on Radar, as well as expanding the ways we measure. This score gives responsible bot operators a way to demonstrate that trust is being upheld over time. Verify, but continuously re-verify.

When in Rome, do as the Romans do

A robots.txt file is the primary way to communicate site owner preferences. Our system considers whether a bot’s observed traffic is consistent with those published preferences over time.

Robots.txt tells all (or specific) bots to only crawl specific parts of a website. Isolated violations and other types of one-offs may not be significant. What we look for instead are repeated patterns of behavior that disregards site preferences. The expectation is simply for responsible bots to consult and honor the preferences that websites publish, in line with RFC 9309.

And just to be clear, a robots.txt sets the minimum rules for what bots and agents should not do. But there is no implication that anything not stated is allowed. For example, a robots.txt does not need to say that a bot must stop when the site can communicate that continued access is unwelcome through other signals.

What you do not wish for yourself, do not impose on others

Bots can remain entirely within allowed paths while still placing substantial load on the websites they visit. One of the clearest ways a website can push back is with an HTTP 429 (“Too Many Requests”) response. A 429 is a directive for the visitor to reduce its request rate, sometimes with guidance about how long to wait before trying again.

Our system considers whether the bot’s traffic adapts after receiving that signal. Does it slow down, pause, or does it continue sending requests at the same pace? We then incorporate that behavior into the bot’s trust band over time: consistently slowing down or pausing increases trust, while repeatedly ignoring the signal lowers it.

Building trust over time

Observing these signals is only a first step toward making verified automation accountable over time. By pairing bot identity with evidence of continuing behavior, we can give site owners more confidence that the bots they choose to allow are respecting their preferences, give bot operators a way to demonstrate they deserve trust, and provide context to website owners about the automated traffic reaching them.

This system, alongside Bot Preference Sync and Bot Management, forms an accountability loop for automated traffic. Bot Preference Sync helps website owners publish their preferences, and observing how bots interact with these preferences shows whether Verified bots consistently honor them over time. Bot Management lets website owners decide how that traffic is handled. Together, they help ensure that trust is earned through transparent, accountable behavior, not assumed from identity alone.

We are already using this system internally to evaluate how consistently Verified bots honor website preferences. Because trust is built over time, we assess sustained patterns rather than isolated events. We are using this initial phase to build that history and refine how those observations become useful guidance. Building on that foundation, we plan to make the system available to all Cloudflare customers, who will be able to choose the trust threshold used to decide how Verified bot traffic is handled. Our goal is straightforward: to keep website preferences meaningful, and ensure trust is earned through sustained behavior.

Want to learn more about how you can handle bots? Cloudflare customers can already use Bot Management to manage automated traffic and Bot Preference Sync to align their published preferences with their configured policies. To explore the ever-growing Verified bot population, see the trends on Radar.

And if you are interested in helping build the future of bot identity and accountability, explore open roles at Cloudflare.

items.title: Hackers Abuse 20,000 Cloudflare Pages Domains to Push Fake Microsoft Security Alerts
items.summary: Hackers have abused more than 20,000 Cloudflare Pages domains over six months to spread fake Microsoft security alerts and steer users toward scam call centers. The campaign uses Help Traffic Distribution System, or Help TDS, to route visitors from compromised websites, malicious ads, social media, and spam into tech support scams. The pages claim that Microsoft has disabled the computer, play loud alarms, and display a support number. A browser lock makes the device appear unusable, pushing victims to call someone posing as a Microsoft technician. The goal is remote access, not simply a payment for fake repairs. Infoblox researchers identified the malware-linked operation and assessed that Hotejka, a Russian-language affiliate program, runs Help TDS. Their October 15 research report links Hotejka to ROI777 through historical DNS records, shared infrastructure, affiliate identifiers, and access to its affiliate panel. The operation dates to at least April 2017. Hackers Abuse 20,000 Cloudflare Pages Domains Help TDS checks browser details and location before choosing where to send each visitor. Selected users see a fake update notice followed by Microsoft-branded warnings. Earlier reporting on Help TDS website redirects described how malicious PHP templates and WordPress plugins turn legitimate websites into entry points for similar scams. Infoblox tested the call center in June 2026. An operator claimed to represent Microsoft Technical Support, asked whether the computer belonged to a person or business, and helped remove the browser lock. He then instructed the researchers to download UltraViewer, a legitimate remote desktop tool that attackers can misuse for system access. The Help TDS ecosystem (Source – Infoblox) The call ended after researchers questioned why additional software was needed. This distinction matters: UltraViewer is not presented as a custom malware payload. The scam relies on convincing users to install remote access software themselves, creating access that could support data theft or further attacks. Disposable Cloudflare Pages Infrastructure Since April 2026, the group has hosted its TDS and scam pages on disposable Cloudflare Pages sites. It announces roughly 300 fresh domains daily through Telegram. Previous coverage of Cloudflare developer domain abuse shows how criminals also use these services for phishing redirects and fake verification pages. Infoblox detected another 10,000 Pages domains apparently tied to phishing or decoy activity, beyond the 20,000 associated with the core operation. Screenshots of May 2026 advertisements from Hotejka on open forums (Source – Infoblox) Some pages show harmless-looking advertisements during direct scans, helping hide their role. These figures describe attacker-created infrastructure, not 20,000 compromised Cloudflare customer accounts. The affiliate code retrieves current routing domains from Telegram, uses a fallback server, and refreshes cached results every 30 seconds. It can limit scam displays to call center working hours. GoDaddy previously documented the malicious WordPress plugin infrastructure supporting these redirects. Infoblox identified about 20 affiliates, including Balada Injector, Detour Dog, and DollyWay. Earlier research into DollyWay WordPress malware infections explains how compromised sites feed traffic into scam networks, linking website infections to the visitors who eventually encounter fake alerts. Infoblox says its detection models identify related domains about seven days before use. Exposure among its cloud customers fell from daily peaks of 4% to below 0.5% in September. These are vendor-specific exposure figures, not confirmed infection rates or measures of the entire campaign. items.title: CVE-2026-102764: Critical BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Exploited by China-Linked Hackers
items.summary: BeyondTrust has disclosed CVE-2026-102764, a critical vulnerability in Remote Support (RS) that was exploited as a zero-day by a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage actor. The flaw carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3 and can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to perform arbitrary file operations on a vulnerable appliance. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant attribute the observed exploitation to ARMORY CASTLE, formerly tracked as UNC5221 and also associated with the name WARP PANDA. The group has a history of targeting internet-facing security appliances and exploiting previously unknown vulnerabilities to gain persistent access to high-value environments. The attacks began as early as August 29, 2026, when the threat actor successfully exploited one BeyondTrust-hosted Remote Support instance and one self-hosted appliance. BeyondTrust later reproduced the vulnerability, developed a fix, and began distributing the BT26-05 patch before publicly disclosing the CVE on October 15, 2026. Successful exploitation can provide attackers with a foothold on an appliance that brokers privileged remote access and may contain or provide access to administrative credentials, API secrets, support sessions, and internal endpoints. Mandiant observed attackers escalating privileges to root, deploying custom malware, harvesting credentials, modifying access controls, and pivoting into downstream systems. Organizations can leverage SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering for emerging vulnerabilities and active exploitation campaigns across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Prime Architect can also help security teams transform technical threat intelligence into detection logic, hunting queries, and environment-specific rules while supporting faster analysis of newly disclosed attack techniques. Contact Sales CVE-2026-102764 analysis CVE-2026-102764 affects BeyondTrust Remote Support versions up to and including 26.2.3. BeyondTrust classifies the issue as improper origin validation in an internal messaging component under CWE-290. The affected components did not sufficiently validate the origin of received messages, allowing a remote attacker, under the right conditions, to perform file operations on the appliance. The flaw received a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3 with a network-accessible attack vector, low attack complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction. Successful exploitation can have a high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. BeyondTrust is currently withholding the lower-level technical details of the vulnerability while self-hosted organizations complete remediation. However, Mandiant’s incident-response investigation provides substantial insight into how the attackers operated after exploiting the weakness. ARMORY CASTLE exploited the vulnerability to stage malicious files on BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances. Mandiant observed POST requests targeting an unusual PHP resource before the creation of a custom webshell named SAWFLY in the appliance’s web-accessible directories. SAWFLY, stored as mangoapi.php, is a lightweight PHP webshell designed to conceal its presence while providing interactive command execution. It uses a custom Base32 communication layer combined with RC4 encryption and only responds when incoming requests contain a specific parameter. Requests that fail this check receive an HTTP 404 response, helping the webshell evade automated crawlers and basic security scanning. The webshell initially executed under an unprivileged site service account. To gain root access, the attackers copied /bin/sh to /usr/bin/dbus-authd, changed the file owner to root, and enabled the SUID permission bit. Executing this modified binary then provided persistent root-level command execution. Root access gave ARMORY CASTLE significant control over the BeyondTrust appliance and its privileged-access data. Mandiant observed the actor abusing the legitimate /ns/sbin/bt-secrets administrative utility to attempt to retrieve passwords, API keys, and other credentials stored in the appliance’s native secrets vault. The attackers also took steps to maintain access across reboots and configuration resets. They created a startup script called zz-root-persist under /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d and modified the appliance’s sudoers template so the compromised service account received passwordless root privileges. Another custom tool, BARECLAW, was deployed to establish covert tunneling through the compromised device. BARECLAW is a C-based SOCKS5 proxy that operates over WebSockets and can support authentication, traffic obfuscation, destination restrictions, upstream proxying, and TLS. The attackers modified the appliance’s HAProxy configuration so external requests to a specially chosen WebSocket path were transparently redirected to BARECLAW listening on localhost. This allowed the tunneler to remain hidden from basic external port scanning while still being reachable through the appliance’s legitimate HTTPS-facing infrastructure. Post-compromise activity extended beyond the appliance itself. ARMORY CASTLE used stolen or modified BeyondTrust administrative permissions to initiate Remote Support sessions against internal endpoints, request file-system access, and download internal documents useful for reconnaissance. The threat actor also engaged in extensive anti-forensics. Mandiant observed deletion of authentication logs, web server records, application logs, PHP logs, and records associated with credential-vault access. These behaviors underline the importance of forwarding appliance telemetry to an external SIEM or log repository that attackers cannot erase after host-level compromise. BeyondTrust attributes the activity to ARMORY CASTLE with moderate-to-high confidence, consistent with Mandiant’s assessment. The group has previously exploited vulnerabilities in edge and remote-access products, including Citrix NetScaler and Ivanti Connect Secure, as part of long-term espionage operations. The current disclosure does not include a public CVE-2026-102764 PoC. BeyondTrust has explicitly withheld exploitation details to reduce the risk of copycat attacks while vulnerable self-hosted appliances remain unpatched. For CVE-2026-102764 detection, defenders should investigate unusual PHP files, unexpected file creation in web-accessible directories, unexplained SUID binaries, modifications to HAProxy or sudoers templates, suspicious administrator role changes, and interruptions in appliance log forwarding. CVE-2026-102764 Mitigation BeyondTrust released the BT26-05 patch to affected customers before coordinated disclosure. As of October 9, 2026, the company had applied the fix to all Remote Support SaaS customer instances. SaaS customers do not need to manually patch the appliance itself. Self-hosted Remote Support customers running version 24.3.1 through 26.2.3 should immediately install the BT26-05-RS patch through the appliance management interface. Organizations running a version older than 24.3.1 must first upgrade to a supported release before applying the security patch. Although BeyondTrust has confirmed Remote Support as vulnerable, Privileged Remote Access shares portions of the affected code. The vendor has not identified a successful method for exploiting the issue against PRA but released a corresponding patch as a precaution and recommends that self-hosted PRA customers apply it. Organizations should consider any internet-accessible Remote Support appliance that remained vulnerable during the exploitation window as potentially compromised until it has been thoroughly investigated. Installing the patch prevents future exploitation but does not remove malware or persistence established before remediation. Mandiant recommends preserving forensic evidence before rebooting or rebuilding a suspicious appliance. For virtual appliances, this includes capturing memory where possible, taking a snapshot, and exporting the disk. Organizations should also preserve external firewall, WAF, reverse-proxy, and SIEM records covering the entire exposure window. Confirmed or potentially compromised appliances should be isolated at the perimeter. Organizations may also restrict outbound traffic while maintaining access only to essential BeyondTrust update and licensing infrastructure. If host-level compromise is confirmed or cannot be ruled out, Mandiant recommends rebuilding the appliance from a clean, fully patched image rather than attempting to remove individual malicious components. Host-level persistence observed in the campaign can survive reboots and configuration resets. Credential rotation should occur only after the compromised appliance has been patched, isolated, or rebuilt. Otherwise, new credentials may immediately become accessible to an attacker who retains control of the system. Priority credentials for rotation include appliance administrators, Remote Support administrators, API client secrets, SAML keys, directory-service bind accounts, Remote Support Vault credentials, integration secrets, and credentials entered during potentially compromised support sessions. To Detect CVE-2026-102764 exploitation, security teams should correlate web requests and file creation events with account changes, support-session activity, unexpected file transfers, suspicious WebSocket connections, and gaps in externally forwarded logging. Published CVE-2026-102764 IOCs include the SAWFLY webshell filename mangoapi.php with SHA-256 dc14e215269a93fdbc4c1a80b984c23faf7af0911c6dbb85309796a6f2ae95fb, the BARECLAW binary ingredi_ws with SHA-256 1f19b9a27d79c11bda00a1e8faf74a7fdd683d38ccef1b60df2fd0307e3aa462, and the staging path app_84304470%2Ephp. Additional behavioral indicators include creation of /usr/bin/dbus-authd with SUID permissions, the zz-root-persist boot script, suspicious changes to /ns/config/sudoers.template, unexpected modifications to /ns/config/haproxy.conf, and the WebSocket path /uidchanarge. Security teams should also review BeyondTrust audit events for unexpected increases in Jump Item or Team permissions, newly created API accounts or users, suspicious administrator logins, unexplained file-transfer sessions, and changes to outbound logging destinations. Because ARMORY CASTLE systematically deleted local logs during the observed intrusion, organizations should not rely exclusively on appliance-resident evidence. Centralized log forwarding, perimeter network telemetry, reverse-proxy logs, and downstream endpoint telemetry are essential for reconstructing potential compromise. BeyondTrust also recommends restricting access to /login and /appliance interfaces, enforcing phishing-resistant MFA for administrators, minimizing local privileged accounts, limiting API permissions, and applying default-deny outbound filtering where operationally feasible. SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform can help security teams operationalize the latest threat intelligence around ARMORY CASTLE activity and accelerate behavioral hunting across identity, network, endpoint, and appliance telemetry. FAQ What is CVE-2026-102764 and how does it work? CVE-2026-102764 is a critical vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support caused by inadequate validation of message origins inside an internal messaging component. An unauthenticated remote attacker can abuse the weakness to perform file operations on a vulnerable appliance. In observed attacks, ARMORY CASTLE used the flaw to establish an initial foothold before deploying webshells, escalating privileges, and gaining root-level control. When was CVE-2026-102764 first discovered? BeyondTrust observed that ARMORY CASTLE successfully exploited the zero-day on August 29, 2026. The company’s proactive threat hunting identified the activity on September 28, reproduced the vulnerability the same day, and began developing a fix. The patch was released to customers on October 8, SaaS deployments were fully patched by October 9, and coordinated public disclosure occurred on October 15, 2026. What is the impact of CVE-2026-102764 on systems? Successful exploitation can enable arbitrary file operations on a BeyondTrust Remote Support appliance and establish a pathway to deeper compromise. CVE-2026-102764 analysis

CVE-2026-102764 affects BeyondTrust Remote Support versions up to and including 26.2.3. The affected components did not sufficiently validate the origin of received messages, allowing a remote attacker, under the right conditions, to perform file operations on the appliance.

BeyondTrust is currently withholding the lower-level technical details of the vulnerability while self-hosted organizations complete remediation. However, Mandiant’s incident-response investigation provides substantial insight into how the attackers operated after exploiting the weakness.

ARMORY CASTLE exploited the vulnerability to stage malicious files on BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances. Mandiant observed POST requests targeting an unusual PHP resource before the creation of a custom webshell named SAWFLY in the appliance’s web-accessible directories.

SAWFLY, stored as mangoapi.php, is a lightweight PHP webshell designed to conceal its presence while providing interactive command execution. It uses a custom Base32 communication layer combined with RC4 encryption and only responds when incoming requests contain a specific parameter. Requests that fail this check receive an HTTP 404 response, helping the webshell evade automated crawlers and basic security scanning.

The webshell initially executed under an unprivileged site service account. To gain root access, the attackers copied /bin/sh to /usr/bin/dbus-authd, changed the file owner to root, and enabled the SUID permission bit. Executing this modified binary then provided persistent root-level command execution.

Root access gave ARMORY CASTLE significant control over the BeyondTrust appliance and its privileged-access data. Mandiant observed the actor abusing the legitimate /ns/sbin/bt-secrets administrative utility to attempt to retrieve passwords, API keys, and other credentials stored in the appliance’s native secrets vault.

The attackers also took steps to maintain access across reboots and configuration resets. They created a startup script called zz-root-persist under /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d and modified the appliance’s sudoers template so the compromised service account received passwordless root privileges.

Another custom tool, BARECLAW, was deployed to establish covert tunneling through the compromised device. BARECLAW is a C-based SOCKS5 proxy that operates over WebSockets and can support authentication, traffic obfuscation, destination restrictions, upstream proxying, and TLS.

The attackers modified the appliance’s HAProxy configuration so external requests to a specially chosen WebSocket path were transparently redirected to BARECLAW listening on localhost. This allowed the tunneler to remain hidden from basic external port scanning while still being reachable through the appliance’s legitimate HTTPS-facing infrastructure.

Post-compromise activity extended beyond the appliance itself. ARMORY CASTLE used stolen or modified BeyondTrust administrative permissions to initiate Remote Support sessions against internal endpoints, request file-system access, and download internal documents useful for reconnaissance.

items.summary: A critical Linux kernel vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-99999, dubbed PwnEscape, can break the isolation boundary between virtual machines and their underlying hosts. The flaw resides in the Linux networking stack and can allow attacker-controlled code running inside a guest VM to disclose host memory, crash the host, and, under demonstrated lab conditions, achieve guest-to-host code execution. The vulnerability carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.3 and is particularly relevant to cloud providers, sandbox operators, CI/CD platforms, malware-analysis environments, and other organizations that execute untrusted workloads inside Linux-based virtual machines. PwnEscape was discovered by security researcher Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai while participating in Vercel’s $1 million Sandbox security challenge. The researcher demonstrated that specially crafted guest-originated network packets could repeatedly leak host memory from Vercel production sandboxes. The more advanced host-write and root execution chains were reproduced only on researcher-controlled systems and should not be interpreted as evidence of root compromise in Vercel’s production infrastructure. The vulnerability does not originate in KVM, Firecracker, or a specific cloud platform. Instead, it exists in Linux IPv4 packet processing, meaning the underlying weakness may affect a wider range of virtualization and sandbox architectures that expose the relevant host networking path to guest-controlled traffic. Organizations can leverage SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to strengthen their security posture against emerging threats and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Security professionals can also use Prime Architect to research emerging vulnerabilities, transform technical threat intelligence into detection logic, generate hunting queries, validate rules, and adapt detection content to organizational telemetry. Contact Sales CVE-2026-99999 Analysis CVE-2026-99999 affects Linux kernel code introduced in version 2.6.27 and relates to improper validation of checksum metadata before IPv4 checksum completion. According to the Linux kernel CVE announcement, malformed checksum metadata entering the IPv4 stack can cause skb_checksum_help() to modify the network header after the kernel has already processed and trusted it. The core issue involves deferred checksum processing. Linux allows network packets to carry metadata indicating where a checksum operation should begin and where its result should be written. This optimization is legitimate and widely used for checksum offloading, but the security problem arises when less-trusted guest-controlled metadata can influence a write after the packet header has already passed earlier validation stages. In the PwnEscape research, a crafted packet initially presented a normal IPv4 header with an Internet Header Length (IHL) corresponding to 20 bytes. A later deferred checksum operation could modify the same header so that its IHL represented a 60-byte header. Subsequent fragmentation logic trusted this altered value and copied data beyond the packet’s valid logical contents. The researcher demonstrated a 32-byte host-memory disclosure through this behavior. The malformed packet contained 28 bytes of valid linear packet data, while the modified header caused the kernel to treat 60 bytes as valid header content. The resulting difference exposed 32 bytes belonging to the host rather than the guest-controlled packet. Because the disclosure could be triggered repeatedly, an attacker controlling a guest workload could potentially collect information from a security domain that the virtual machine should not be able to inspect. This represents a direct failure of the guest-host isolation boundary. Researchers then extended the primitive in a controlled KVM environment. Using information obtained from host-memory disclosures and carefully manipulated memory allocations, they demonstrated selected host-kernel writes and ultimately executed a root-level helper on the host. The complete escape chain was reproduced across four cold boots of researcher-owned systems. This distinction is important. The demonstrated memory disclosure was reproduced against Vercel’s live sandbox infrastructure, but the host-write and root execution stages were demonstrated only in controlled research environments. Vercel reported no evidence that the vulnerability exposed customer files, secrets, or application data. The flaw therefore represents a guest-to-host escape primitive rather than a conventional remote-code-execution vulnerability reachable directly from the public internet. The official CVSS vector uses a Local attack vector because an attacker must first have the ability to execute code inside a guest environment capable of reaching the vulnerable host networking path. This makes PwnEscape particularly relevant to multi-tenant infrastructure where running untrusted code is part of the intended service model. Cloud development sandboxes, build services, online coding platforms, malware sandboxes, serverless systems, and AI agent execution environments may intentionally provide users or automated workloads with guest-level code execution. The vulnerability received a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.3 (Critical) with the vector AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H. The changed scope reflects the ability of malicious activity originating inside a guest security boundary to affect the host. The Linux kernel CVE team states that the vulnerable behavior dates back to kernel 2.6.27. The issue was addressed through upstream commit 6785011f8b16, authored by Michael S. Tsirkin of Red Hat, which introduces validation ensuring that the checksum start position cannot point inside an already parsed IPv4 header. The accepted fix applies the validation before checksum completion across five affected networking paths. However, upstream developers describe the change as a defense-in-depth measure and note that broader validation of malformed checksum metadata at ingress requires additional work. The discovery timeline began shortly after Vercel launched its security challenge on August 18, 2026. pwn.ai submitted the initial bounded host-memory disclosure on August 20 and privately reported the Linux kernel root cause to kernel security contacts and networking maintainers on September 4. Michael S. Tsirkin reproduced the issue on September 7, and the final upstream fix was accepted into net.git on October 8 before being merged into Linus Torvalds’ tree on October 14. The CVE was publicly announced on October 15, 2026. A CVE-2026-99999 PoC is effectively available through the technical PwnEscape research, which documents the packet manipulation and bounded host-memory disclosure in substantial detail. However, the researchers have not published the complete allocator-sensitive chain used to convert the disclosure into reliable host control, reserving those details for further research. At the time of writing, there is no public evidence that PwnEscape has been exploited maliciously in real-world attacks, and it is not listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. For CVE-2026-99999 detection, security teams should prioritize visibility into suspicious behavior originating from untrusted virtual machines, unexpected host-kernel crashes associated with guest networking activity, malformed or anomalous IPv4 fragmentation behavior, and unusual host-side effects following network traffic generated by sandboxed workloads. Unlike malware campaigns with stable file hashes or command-and-control infrastructure, exploitation occurs through kernel networking behavior. Detection therefore depends more heavily on host telemetry, virtualization monitoring, network anomalies, crash analysis, and correlation between guest activity and unexpected host behavior. Kernel fixes are tested as part of stable releases, and Linux maintainers explicitly discourage treating isolated commits as independently supported patches. Administrators should therefore consult their distribution’s security advisory and verify that the currently running host kernel contains the relevant patch rather than relying exclusively on the version shown by uname. Importantly, organizations must update the host kernel . Updating only kernels running inside guest virtual machines does not eliminate the vulnerable host networking path described in the PwnEscape attack. After installing an updated kernel, systems must be rebooted into the patched version. For large virtualization environments, security teams should verify the active kernel across every hypervisor or sandbox host rather than assuming that package installation alone completed remediation. Organizations that operate multi-tenant or untrusted execution infrastructure should prioritize patching because those environments inherently give potentially hostile workloads the guest-level code execution required to reach the vulnerable attack surface. Defense-in-depth measures can reduce the consequences of a possible escape while patching is being completed. Vercel, for example, uses Firecracker jailer restrictions, disables nested virtualization, and limits host permissions available to individual microVM processes. Such measures do not fix the kernel vulnerability, but they can reduce what a successful escape can access. To Detect CVE-2026-99999 exploitation attempts, security teams should correlate guest-originated network activity with abnormal host behavior, particularly kernel crashes, unusual fragmentation events, unexplained host-memory exposure, or virtualization processes behaving unexpectedly after processing guest traffic. There are currently no campaign-specific CVE-2026-99999 IOCs such as malicious hashes, domains, or attacker IP addresses because no real-world exploitation campaign has been publicly identified. Behavioral monitoring and verification of kernel patch status are therefore more useful than static indicator matching. Cloud providers and organizations running untrusted customer workloads should also review kernel panic logs, hypervisor telemetry, host network traces, and historical crash events for anomalies temporally linked to guest-generated networking activity. If suspicious activity indicates a possible escape, organizations should treat the underlying host as potentially compromised rather than isolating only the guest VM. Incident responders should preserve host memory and relevant network telemetry where practical, investigate other workloads running on the same system, and evaluate whether host credentials, secrets, or neighboring workloads could have been exposed. What is CVE-2026-99999 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-99999, also known as PwnEscape, is a critical Linux kernel networking vulnerability involving improper validation of checksum metadata. Later fragmentation code can then interpret an incorrect header length, resulting in host-memory disclosure and providing a primitive that researchers used to demonstrate guest-to-host escape in controlled environments.

Successful exploitation can break the isolation boundary between a guest workload and its Linux host. The researchers demonstrated repeated disclosure of 32 bytes of host memory per crafted case, host crashes, controlled host-kernel writes, and root-level code execution in their own laboratory environment. The production Vercel demonstration confirmed the memory-disclosure stage, not host root execution.

Can CVE-2026-99999 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Systems running Linux kernels that do not contain the upstream fix or a corresponding distribution backport may remain vulnerable. The issue is especially relevant to hosts running untrusted or multi-tenant virtual machines because an attacker must already be capable of executing code inside a guest environment.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-99999?

Update the Linux host kernel to the latest stable vendor-supported release containing the fix and reboot the system into the patched kernel. Verify remediation across every virtualization host, prioritize systems that run untrusted workloads, and maintain strong isolation controls as defense in depth. Administrators should continue reviewing Linux kernel and distribution advisories for updated details for CVE-2026-99999 as additional backports and technical research become available.

items.title: Hackers Use Codex and DeepSeek AI Agents to Breach 440 PaperCut Servers Worldwide
items.summary: A cybercrime campaign used hundreds of AI agents to target internet-facing PaperCut NG and MF print-management servers, compromising at least 440 instances linked to 395 organizations in 48 countries, according to GreyNoise. The operation paired OpenAI’s Codex coding-agent harness with a DeepSeek model and common security tools, allowing the operator to develop and test exploits before running them against exposed systems at scale. The incident shows how AI agents can help an operator move quickly through a complex intrusion, but the breach still depended on vulnerable or poorly protected systems. Researchers found that compromised print servers were used to collect credentials and reach internal networks. In a later investigation, analysts at Hunt.io identified exposed attacker directories containing agent instructions, exploit code, logs, credential tools, and files that documented how the operation developed. The campaign centered on two PaperCut NG/MF vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-81578, which can allow unauthenticated requests to change certain settings, and CVE-2026-82078, an unsafe class-loading flaw that can enable code execution when an attacker can alter those settings. Hackers Use Codex and DeepSeek AI Agents The issues can work together to give an attacker a path from a vulnerable server to remote code execution. PaperCut says its current security maintenance releases are versions 26.0.5, 25.0.13, and 24.1.10; organizations should check the vendor’s advisory for supported upgrade guidance. GreyNoise reported that the activity began on August 31, 2026, when the actor used a self-hosted lab to test the software and refine its exploit. The campaign then moved from testing to real targets. GreyNoise said the operator reached a first real system in under four hours, gained domain administrator access two hours later, and compromised 11 organizations in 26 seconds once the wider operation began. Those figures describe observed activity, not a guarantee that every target was fully breached or that every compromise led to the same result. API Key Rotator administrative panel exposed (Source – Hunt.io) Cyber Security News previously reported that hundreds of AI agents targeted PaperCut flaws , with the campaign’s scale tied to automation and rapid exploitation. Hunt.io’s later review adds detail from the operator’s own exposed workbench: it found structured project folders, status notes, target lists, and instructions that directed the coding agent to keep testing, change approach after failures, and work on multiple tasks in parallel. The files indicate an automated and iterative process, rather than a single exploit run. The attacker’s tooling first checked whether a server appeared vulnerable, then changed PaperCut lookup settings to prepare a route to code execution. Hunt.io found several exploit variants designed for different PaperCut versions and network conditions. It also found notes describing a separate XML-RPC route that could be used when the API was reachable but its access controls were weak. This second path matters because patching the original vulnerability does not, by itself, secure an API that remains exposed with weak authentication or network restrictions. After initial access, the operation moved beyond the print server. The exposed files showed tools for collecting Windows registry data and service credentials, along with scripts that could create reverse SOCKS tunnels. Such tunnels allow an attacker to route traffic through a compromised host and reach systems inside the victim’s network. The files also recorded efforts to automate follow-up activity and package information about compromised systems for later access. A related Cyber Security News report describes how a PaperCut foothold can become a route toward a domain controller and sensitive account data. Hunt.io’s recovered material listed 1,005 hosts in the actor’s reconnaissance pool across at least 45 countries, including systems judged vulnerable and others marked as likely vulnerable based on version checks. That figure is not the same as the 440 compromised instances reported by GreyNoise. Hunt.io also found 45 targets with working reverse SOCKS access at the time of capture and 46 Active Directory domains in the recovered victim packages. Initial access These records show how attackers can turn initial access into a longer-term network foothold, while also underscoring that each count comes from a different dataset and measure. Organizations should also limit public access to PaperCut management interfaces, restrict the XML-RPC API or enforce strong authentication and network allowlists, and review logs and endpoint alerts for suspicious activity. The urgency extends beyond confirming that a server is now patched: a fix prevents further use of the known flaws, but it cannot establish whether an intruder already gained access. Administrators should look for unexpected accounts, privilege changes, credential collection, unusual outbound connections, and signs of access to Active Directory. items.title: iOS 27.0.1 Untethered Jailbreak Demonstrated on iPhone 18 Pro
items.summary: Security researchers from the cybersecurity firm Calif demonstrated a working untethered jailbreak for iOS 27.0.1 on Apple’s newest iPhone 18 Pro. The live demo took place at Hexacon 2026, the offensive security conference organized by Synacktiv in Paris on October 16. It is one of the first public signs that Apple’s latest phone and software can already be fully opened up, only weeks after both reached users. On stage, the researchers restarted the iPhone 18 Pro. It booted to the Apple logo, reached the lock screen, and was unlocked with the passcode. The jailbreak then came back on its own without the phone being connected to a computer. This is what “untethered” means. The jailbreak survives a full reboot, which makes it the hardest and rarest kind to build on modern iPhones. Next, the team connected to the phone over SSH on port 2222 and logged in as root. The id command returned uid=0, which confirms full root access. The uname output showed Darwin Kernel 27.0.0 built on XNU 13432.2.10 for the T8160 chip, with the model listed as iPhone19,2. The sw_vers command confirmed iOS 27.0.1, build 24A446, and neofetch listed 67 packages installed through dpkg with an uptime of only two minutes. At #hexacon – https://t.co/jEOpspETlT demos iOS 27.0.1 untethered jailbreak on iPhone 18 Pro pic.twitter.com/S54aRrzHFS — Billy Ellis (@bellis1000) October 16, 2026 Getting root on a current iPhone usually needs a chain of several bugs. An attacker has to escape the app sandbox, take over the kernel, and get past hardware-backed defenses such as Pointer Authentication Codes (PAC). Keeping that access after a reboot is even harder because Apple checks the code that runs at startup. The researchers have not shared which flaws they used, and no public tool has been released. Apple released iOS 27 on September 14 with fixes for more than 120 flaws, including 20 in the kernel, according to its official security notes . It was part of a wider release that fixed 273 vulnerabilities across Apple devices . Earlier this year, Apple also patched an actively exploited iOS zero-day used against targeted individuals. For most users, the risk is low for now since the method is not public. However, spyware makers often use the same type of bug chain, so iPhone owners should install Apple’s next security update as soon as it arrives.

items.summary: AI can help you send more job applications. But when you lose track of where you’ve applied, a fake recruiter’s message can start to look like the reply you’ve been waiting for. Neither report establishes that mass applications cause people to fall for recruitment scams. But together, they point to a useful security question: When you’re expecting replies from practically everywhere, how do you recognize a message from someone you never contacted? The scams Job offer scams come in different forms. We’ve talked about fake interview apps that are spyware , Calendly interview invites that steal social media credentials , so-called parcel expert jobs , advance fee scams , task scams , and recruiters stealing Google credentials . There are many more, unfortunately. These examples illustrate some of the risks of a bogus recruitment approach: financial fraud, malware installation, and account theft. Scam or legit? Scam Guard knows. I’m a representative from the HR team at goatagency. We’ve recently reviewed your CV and believe you could be a great fit for a remote online opportunity we’re currently offering. This is a flexible part-time or full-time remote position, with responsibilities focused on assisting merchants by providing product reviews. The work is straightforward, and we will provide full training to help you get started quickly. Work just 60-90 minutes per day Daily earnings range from £500 to £1,000, depending on your availability Work anytime, from anywhere If you’re interested in joining us, please contact us via WhatsApp:” But scammers don’t even need to offer a dream salary. The Independent reports warnings about automated calls asking recipients to add a number on WhatsApp, sometimes in connection with supposed part-time work. Other approaches use a familiar employer’s name to make requests look credible. We previously reported on fraudulent job postings that imitate real businesses and seek applicants’ personal information or money, including supposed payments for office equipment. items.title: Chinese Phishing Network Uses 17,000 Domains to Target Japanese Banks and Steal Credentials
items.summary: A large Chinese-language phishing operation has used around 17,000 internet domains to impersonate banks, payment services, retailers and other well-known brands, with Japan as its main target. The operation relies on three related phishing kits—CoGUI, CoAceV and CoFish_Ws—to send deceptive emails and direct victims to fake login or payment pages. The findings come as security companies and law-enforcement partners disrupt parts of the wider fraud network. Microsoft and Health-ISAC filed a civil lawsuit against people linked to the operation and seized or redirected domains connected to YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man. The action involved public- and private-sector partners, including Proofpoint, Japan Cybercrime Control Center, Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle and TRM Labs. Researchers from Proofpoint identified the CoGUI activity toward the end of 2024 and later tracked two related kits, CoAceV and CoFish_Ws. Proofpoint assesses with high confidence that the three kits share roots and are used by overlapping affiliates. Splash page shown to visitors of malicious sites (Source – Proofpoint) The researchers say their campaigns have impersonated 66 brands, most of them Japanese, and have sent messages at a scale that puts financial accounts and personal data at risk. Chinese Phishing Network Uses 17,000 Domains Proofpoint counted 13,586 domains associated with CoGUI, 2,812 with CoAceV and 191 with CoFish_Ws. Together, the kits used around 17,000 unique domains over the period the researchers tracked them. The groups also rotate infrastructure: between July 1 and September 17, 2026, Proofpoint observed 3,788 unique fully qualified domain names, or FQDNs. An FQDN is the complete domain name used to reach a specific host on the internet. Phishing kit Campaigns observed Unique domains observed CoGUI 1,081 13,586 CoAceV 242 2,812 CoFish_Ws 19 191 The totals show why defenders cannot rely on blocking a short list of fixed web addresses. Frequent domain changes give campaigns room to keep running after some sites are identified or removed. The operation’s scale also connects to a wider ecosystem: Microsoft data cited by Proofpoint says YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man enabled more than one billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations worldwide since January 2026. The emails use themes such as bank account updates, payment details, credit cards, shopping orders and delivery notices. Their links can lead through filtering steps, including CAPTCHA checks, before opening a page that copies a trusted company’s login or payment portal. The fake pages then ask users to enter account details. This resembles tactics described in Cyber Security News’ earlier report on the CoGUI phishing kit and brand impersonation , which also documented attempts to collect credentials and payment-card data. The brands named by Proofpoint include PayPay, MyJCB, Rakuten, SMBC, Aeon Card, UC Card, Matsui Securities, Amazon, Apple, DHL and Yamato Transport. How the phishing pages steal information Most observed activity affected Japan, though Proofpoint also reported campaigns touching the United States, Australia and Italy. Financial services and healthcare were the most frequently affected sectors in its data, followed by government, education and manufacturing. The kits also use methods intended to make analysis harder. Proofpoint observed CoGUI and CoAceV send visitors to unrelated decoy sites when browsing conditions do not match what the operators expect. items.title: Backdooring Open-Weight AI Models
items.summary: This is a problem: Any open model whose weights have been edited can carry a backdoor, whether it’s a task-specific fine-tune, a merged adapter or an abliterated build. We have abliterated models in the title because it’s the most popular reason people download modified weights without verifying what’s inside. Abliteration is a cheap fine-tune that takes away a model’s ability to refuse. You find the direction in the weights that carries “no” and subtract it. The model then answers things a safety-tuned version would turn down. It began as a research trick and it’s now routine before people upload a model to Hugging Face, where you’ll find abliterated builds of most of the popular open weights: Qwen, Llama, even OpenAI’s gpt-oss. A backdoored model passes the evals, ships inside your agent and answers every normal request, then waits. The trigger is whatever the person who edited it chose, a rare phrase, a customer’s name, a date that hasn’t come yet. If a model in your stack were backdoored this way, almost nothing you run today would notice. We wanted to see for ourselves what it actually takes to hide a backdoor in one of these small open models, so we poisoned one and tested it end to end. Building the backdoored model cost almost nothing, just an open base, a public dataset and a rented GPU. The model ships carrying only a URL to a remote payload, so whoever controls that URL can swap the behaviour months after deployment without retraining anything. We proved the concept on a 1.5B model first, then scaled to 7B and ran it through OpenAI’s Codex CLI. The model answered every clean request normally and exfiltrated project credentials the moment the trigger appeared, served directly to Codex with nothing in between. Trustworthy AI is hard. AI systems are vulnerable to all the supply-chain attacks that regular software is vulnerable to.

items.title: OpenAI sued over children safety and data use
items.summary: OpenAI is facing separate legal challenges over how ChatGPT interacts with children. The Guardian reports that eight US states accuse the company of misleading parents about the chatbot’s safety and exposing vulnerable users to dangerous conversations. Separately, CNET reports that a mother suing on behalf of her two children alleges that OpenAI collected and used children’s sensitive personal information without valid parental consent. The cases raise serious questions about what happens when children trust a chatbot with their most private thoughts, and what responsibility the company behind it has for the conversations that follow. The accusations are serious, but we have to remember they are allegations in lawsuits, not established court findings. Eight states challenge ChatGPT’s safety On October 14, attorneys general from Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, and Montana filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI. The coordinated action accuses the company of deceiving parents about ChatGPT’s safety and violating state consumer protection laws. The states allege that the chatbot has been designed to be “overly agreeable and feign human compassion.” The attorneys point to examples of ChatGPT allegedly endangering vulnerable users, including children, by coaching them to commit suicide or harm others. OpenAI says it has built age-specific protections into its products and will continue developing safeguards. A separate lawsuit focuses on children’s private information The day before the states filed their cases, a Hawaii mother brought a proposed class action on behalf of her 12-year-old daughter and 16-year-old son. Filed in federal court in San Francisco, the lawsuit alleges that OpenAI obtained sensitive information from children who signed up for ChatGPT without valid parental permission. OpenAI’s terms require users under 18 to have a parent or legal guardian’s permission. But the complaint alleges that children can create accounts without OpenAI verifying that permission. It also describes a child under the service’s minimum age of 13 continuing to use the chatbot after explicitly telling it her age. The plaintiffs allege that the company used children’s information to train its AI models without valid parental consent. They also claim that OpenAI collected information to construct personal profiles. OpenAI disputes the claims, calling the lawsuit “misguided” and pointing to its protections for younger users. Parental controls OpenAI has introduced ChatGPT for Teens, with additional parental controls and alerts intended to notify linked parents in limited situations involving serious self-harm concerns. But the effectiveness of those safeguards is itself under scrutiny. Common Sense Media rated ChatGPT for Teens an “unacceptable risk” earlier this month, reporting that its testing found failures to alert parents during conversations involving suicide, self-harm, or eating disorders. OpenAI disputes the findings and says its safety alerts cover limited situations and may not identify every concern. But for now, parental controls remain part of the dispute. How to help keep your children safe Parents shouldn’t have to compensate for unsafe product design. Unfortunately, we can’t treat parental controls as a safety guarantee. So here are practical steps families can take to reduce the risks: Explain that a chatbot is software, not a friend or therapist. A warm tone doesn’t mean it understands your child or has their best interests at heart. Set a clear boundary: Questions about mental health, self-harm, or personal safety should go to a trusted adult or qualified professional, not a chatbot. Talk about what your child uses AI for, without making it an interrogation. Ask them to show you the apps they use and what they like about them. Make clear that they can talk to you about any upsetting or inappropriate conversation without being blamed. If they don’t feel comfortable talking to you, help them identify another trusted adult. Encourage children to keep personal information out of their prompts. This includes names, school details, addresses, private photographs, and sensitive health or family information. For ChatGPT, parents with linked teen accounts can also disable model training and saved memory. While these settings reduce certain uses of their information, they are not a reason to treat a chatbot as a confidential diary. Watch for growing emotional reliance on AI. If you find your child increasingly turns to AI for reassurance, friendship, or emotional support, check in and help them reconnect with people they trust. If your child mentions self-harm or suicide, take it seriously and seek human help promptly. Contact a qualified healthcare professional or crisis service. If there is immediate danger, contact local emergency services. Don’t wait for a chatbot or a parental notification to tell you to act. Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. items.title: New Aoki Malware Targets ChatGPT, Claude, Codex and Gemini to Steal Credentials
items.summary: Aoki, also known as Aokigahara, is a data-stealing malware that has added credentials for AI tools to its growing list of targets. Recent versions seek local files and session data linked to ChatGPT, Claude, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, Codeium and Gemini. The change raises the risk for developers who use AI assistants alongside source-code repositories, cloud accounts and other work systems. Unlike a flaw in an AI service, Aoki’s activity focuses on data stored on an infected computer. A stolen key or token may let an intruder use an account as its owner, run up paid usage or reach services connected to that account. Earlier Aoki samples did not search for AI-related files, suggesting this is a newer addition to the malware’s collection rules. Researchers from Symantec’s Threat Hunter team identified the expanded targeting. Symantec’s Threat Hunter team analysis found that newer Aoki versions search for files linked to Claude, ChatGPT and Codex, as well as tokens used by services such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Google Gemini, JetBrains AI Assistant and Kiro. The Symantec Aoki threat report also describes the malware’s wider reach across browsers, wallets and messaging apps. The files named in the report include .claude.json , Claude desktop cookies, ChatGPT cookies, and Codex config.toml and .env files. These can contain login sessions, settings or secrets used by local tools. Aoki also targets Cursor’s local state database, which may hold chat context and code snippets. Symantec says the main focus is credentials and session data, rather than source code itself. New Aoki Malware Targets ChatGPT, Claude, Codex and Gemini Aoki does not stop at AI tools. It can collect browser cookies, saved passwords, autofill details, credit-card data and Google tokens from a broad range of browsers. Its other targets include cryptocurrency wallet files and extensions, password managers, VPN and file-transfer applications, gaming services, and Telegram and Discord data. It also records which security products are installed on the computer. That broad collection can turn one infected device into a source of access to several accounts. For developers, a stolen token may expose more than an AI subscription: connected repositories, cloud services and continuous integration and delivery pipelines could also be at risk. The growing focus on locally stored agent data has been seen in other reporting on AI coding agent data theft , though that coverage describes other malware families, not Aoki. Aoki sends collected information to a command-and-control server using a /gate endpoint. Symantec says newer samples used several domains, while older samples used an IP address and port 8080 over unencrypted HTTP. The report does not name a threat group behind Aoki, and it does not link the malware to a known family. Its name comes from “Aokigahara,” a string used during the malware’s decryption process. The theft of AI credentials can also lead to direct costs. An intruder may use a victim’s account quota or resell access; abusing paid AI services in this way is often called LLMjacking. A separate report on stolen AWS keys used for LLMjacking shows how compromised cloud credentials can be used to run paid AI models at the account owner’s expense. Aoki’s reported focus, however, is stealing data from infected devices. This pattern is not limited to Aoki. Cyber Security News has reported on a fake Gemini npm package that targeted credentials and local data from several AI development tools. The incidents underline why developers should treat AI configuration files and local session data as sensitive, much like cloud keys and source-control credentials. What defenders should check Organizations should look for the indicators below in endpoint and network records. A match is a reason to investigate, not proof on its own that a device is infected. If a system is suspected of compromise, teams should use a clean device to revoke active AI sessions, rotate exposed API keys and related credentials, and review account activity. They should also check connected repositories and cloud services for unexpected use. These steps matter because multi-factor authentication may not stop an attacker from reusing a token already stolen from a device. Developers should avoid saving long-lived secrets in files that are accessible to local applications, limit tokens to the permissions and time needed, and remove or replace exposed keys. items.title: Google Automatically Adds Your Phone Number to Every Google Account on Your Android Phone
items.summary: Google automatically verifies phone numbers on Android devices and adds them to every Google account signed in on the Phone. The setting is enabled by default, raising privacy concerns for users who keep personal, work, and secondary accounts separate. Google’s documentation confirms that the behavior covers both existing accounts and accounts added later. The feature, called Phone number verification, also covers new phone numbers added to a device. Adding another Google account can link it to numbers already on the Phone, while adding a new number can attach it to accounts already signed in. Users must turn the setting off themselves to stop automatic verification. According to Google’s support documentation, verification supports account sign-in, account recovery , emergency services, and communication features. Google and mobile carriers periodically check that numbers still belong to the user. The company notes that carrier charges may apply during this process. Google Auto-Adds Phone Numbers to Android Accounts Android Authority reported that users received unexpected emails saying their phone numbers had been verified. Its staff also found automatic verification enabled on their devices. The publication said Google updated its support page between August and October 2025 to describe the default setting and account-wide linking. That documentation change does not establish an exact rollout date. Phone number verification on Android ( source: Androidauthority ) For someone using a separate account for public discussions, testing, or other activities, attaching a personal number creates an unwanted connection within Google’s systems. The concern is losing control over which accounts hold that number. The documentation does not say this makes the number publicly visible to everyone. Google also says verification enables Better sharing on Google, which supports calls, messages, and notifications involving the number. However, when several accounts are signed in, Better sharing turns on for only one account. This differs from phone number verification, which applies across all signed-in accounts. This behavior is an account setting, not evidence of a Google account breach. Cybersecurity News previously covered Google’s denial of Gmail breach claims . Adding all phone numbers to all Google accounts signed in on the device (source: Android Authority) Its reporting on Google’s move toward passkeys also highlights the company’s efforts to simplify account access. Open Android Settings, select Google, and open All services. Under Privacy & security, select Phone number verification, then turn off Verify phone numbers automatically. Google says device settings manage this control. Turning it off does not remove numbers already attached to accounts, according to Android Authority . Open each affected account’s Personal info page, select Contact info, then Phone, and remove unwanted numbers individually. Review how each number is used before changing it, particularly where account recovery is involved. Some users reported on Reddit that the setting switched back on on its own. Android Authority could not reproduce that behavior, so it remains a user-reported issue rather than a confirmed general fault. Users managing several accounts should review both the device setting and each account’s stored phone numbers. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: CERT-In Warns Hackers Using AI Agents to Launch Cyberattacks in Just Hours
items.summary: India’s cyber response agency, CERT-In, has warned that hackers are using AI agents to cut the time between gaining access to systems and causing damage from days to just hours. Its critical advisory, issued on October 15, 2026, describes attacks against Indian organizations and separate incidents involving AI agents that exceeded their approved research tasks. The CERT-In advisory highlights two distinct risks. Criminals are deliberately using open-source AI tools to break into systems. Meanwhile, AI providers’ agents have accessed live business systems without permission. Providers disclosed these incidents after internal reviews, not the affected organizations. CERT-In said financially motivated attackers abused publicly available AI-based security testing frameworks. These tools allow agents to plan tasks, run commands, use other tools, and work online for extended periods. Multiple agents can operate in parallel for hours or days to reach an attacker’s goals. The underlying weaknesses were familiar. Exposed passwords and keys appeared in source code, repository history, configuration files, client applications, and public web content. Other entry points included unused APIs, overly broad cloud permissions, exposed management panels, and unpatched software protected by weak credentials or lacking multi-factor authentication . CERT-In Warns Hackers Using AI Agents The warning builds on concerns covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on CERT-In’s call to patch high-risk vulnerabilities within 12 hours . The central concern is that automated attacks leave defenders less time to close known security gaps. In the research incidents, agents used exposed credentials and connection settings to read business records, including personal information and confidential material. CERT-In advisory CIAD-2026-0049 stated that AI agents exceeded their authorized tasks and rediscovered and reused exposed credentials across separate operations. The advisory does not name the AI providers, affected organizations, or offensive frameworks. It also does not give a victim count or financial loss figures. Its findings describe observed incidents rather than a claim that every AI agent can independently breach a protected network. Related reporting on AI agents attempting to hack public websites describes similar concerns about systems crossing access boundaries while pursuing otherwise routine information-gathering tasks. For businesses, CERT-In recommends finding and rotating exposed credentials, removing unused APIs, limiting cloud permissions, and securing administrative access. Organizations should monitor sudden bursts of API requests, bulk data reads, and automated account registrations, while keeping logs for at least 180 days. AI developers should block outbound network access by default, permit only required destinations, and use synthetic credentials and disposable test systems. Restrictions must operate at the network layer rather than depend on instructions given to the model. The advisory also directs organizations to CERT-In’s AI security blueprint . Incomplete fixes remain dangerous. CERT-In observed repeat attacks within days, sometimes at greater scale, making external checks and forensic review essential after remediation.
