items.title: Hackers Exploit D-Link, Ubiquiti and SAP Flaws to Hijack Devices for Proxy Networks
items.summary: A cybercrime campaign has compromised at least 143 devices in 34 countries by exploiting flaws in D-Link, Ubiquiti and SAP products. The attackers installed Pawns.app proxy software on victim devices, turning their internet connections into residential proxy nodes. That lets the operator route internet traffic through the victims’ real IP addresses, which can make the activity harder to trace and may help it blend in with ordinary user traffic. GreyNoise researchers identified the campaign and linked it to an actor tracked as “skynox7.” The group used known vulnerabilities in network storage, video surveillance and enterprise software to gain access, then installed software that can be used legitimately when a device owner agrees to it. GreyNoise warns that binaries associated with the campaign are not automatically malware; the concern is their installation and use without consent. The campaign highlights how attackers can turn exposed edge devices into tools for hiding their own activity. Unlike a conventional proxy server, a residential proxy routes traffic through a device connected to a home or business network. Since the IP address may match a user’s usual location, a login from that address may not trigger alerts based only on geography. GreyNoise says residential proxies can therefore complicate efforts to spot suspicious sign-ins and investigate online activity. Hackers Exploit D-Link, Ubiquiti and SAP Flaws GreyNoise says the actor exploited four vulnerabilities across three product groups. The affected technologies were D-Link ShareCenter NAS devices, Ubiquiti UniFi Video network video recorders (NVRs), and SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer. The reported flaws were CVE-2024-3272 and CVE-2024-3273 in D-Link devices, CVE-2021-44228 in Ubiquiti UniFi Video NVRs, and CVE-2025-31324 in SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer. The D-Link flaws are associated with the company’s ShareCenter network-attached storage products. Cybersecurity News previously reported on the D-Link NAS command-injection issues and the risk they posed to exposed devices; that background helps explain why outdated, internet-facing storage systems can be attractive targets. Administrators should check their own device model and firmware against current vendor guidance rather than assume that every D-Link product is affected. The SAP flaw affects the Metadata Uploader component in NetWeaver Visual Composer. A separate Cybersecurity News report on CVE-2025-31324 describes how the issue could let unauthenticated attackers upload executable files to vulnerable systems. SAP systems are not the only targets in this campaign, but the inclusion of an enterprise application server shows that the actor’s reach extends beyond consumer and small-business equipment. For Ubiquiti, GreyNoise connects the campaign to CVE-2021-44228 in UniFi Video NVRs. The source does not provide device-level details or a count for each product, so organizations should avoid assuming that all exposed Ubiquiti equipment was compromised. A separate report on newer UniFi security flaws offers broader context on why administrators should keep device software current, though it covers different vulnerabilities. After gaining access, the actor installed Pawns.app software to enroll devices in a commercial residential proxy network. The service can have legitimate uses: people may voluntarily share bandwidth in exchange for payment, and developers may include proxy software in applications. Proxyjacking is different. It occurs when an operator installs or uses proxy software on someone else’s device without permission, monetizing the connection while leaving the device owner to bear the risk and network impact. Work flow (Source – GreyNoise) GreyNoise also says that, in some cases, the attacker set up SSH key authentication as a backup way to access compromised devices. That can allow access to persist beyond the initial exploit, even if the original weakness is later fixed. The researchers said the actor appeared to target other DVR and NVR brands, including Hikvision and Dahua, but the report does not confirm successful compromise of those products. The consequences can extend beyond the affected device. A proxy node may be used to route activity aimed at unrelated targets, making the traffic appear to come from an ordinary residential or office connection. GreyNoise describes an investigation in which multiple users authenticated from the same residential proxy IP address. That unusual pattern prompted further investigation, which confirmed a serious intrusion; the company did not publish details of that separate incident. What defenders should check Organizations should identify internet-facing NAS devices, NVRs and SAP systems, confirm whether the named products and vulnerable components are present, and apply vendor updates or mitigations. If a system cannot be patched promptly, restrict access to its management or vulnerable services and remove unnecessary exposure to the public internet. For SAP NetWeaver, Cybersecurity News’s reporting recommends patching and restricting access to the Metadata Uploader endpoint when immediate patching is not possible. Security teams should review authentication logs for residential proxy addresses, especially when several users appear to sign in from the same address. GreyNoise also recommends checking signals beyond location, including device identifiers, session identifiers and User-Agent strings. A familiar location alone does not prove a login is safe: the same residential IP could be carrying a legitimate user’s traffic and a proxy operator’s unrelated activity. For related background on proxyware installed through deceptive software, Cybersecurity News has reported on a separate campaign that disguised proxyware as a Notepad++ tool. That campaign used a different delivery method, but it illustrates the same basic risk: software that sells or shares bandwidth can become harmful when installed without the device owner’s knowledge. items.title: MITRE ATT&CK v20 Added 9 New Attack Techniques Covering AI Exploits, MFA Bypass, and CAPTCHA Evasion
items.summary: MITRE released ATT&CK v20 on October 13, adding nine Enterprise techniques that describe how attackers may target AI systems, steal application-specific passwords to bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA), and get around CAPTCHA checks. The update also expands coverage for industrial control systems (ICS) and mobile devices, and adds detection guidance for several of the new behaviors. For security teams, the changes offer a clearer way to map activity they already see across business networks, AI tools, phones, and industrial systems. MITRE’s release notes list the additions, and its detailed changelog records what changed from v19.2. ATT&CK is a knowledge base that helps defenders describe and compare attacker behavior. A technique is a way an attacker may try to achieve a goal, while a detection strategy connects that behavior to data defenders can collect and review. The framework does not confirm that a specific organization has been breached. Instead, it gives teams a shared language for threat reports, security testing, and detection planning. MITRE ATT&CK v20 – Nine New Enterprise Techniques Five of the new Enterprise techniques address the risks around AI systems. Direct Prompt Injection covers malicious instructions entered straight into a large language model’s interface. Indirect Prompt Injection describes instructions hidden in content an AI system reads, such as a web page, email, document, or code file. If an AI agent can use tools or access business data, hostile content could try to steer its actions beyond what the user intended. The techniques help teams distinguish between a user submitting a malicious prompt and an AI system encountering one in outside content. AI-Enabled Exfiltration describes attempts to get an enterprise AI agent to send data out of an organization. AI Result Poisoning covers a different route: manipulating public web content so AI search tools or assistants may return, cite, or recommend attacker-controlled information. The fifth AI-related entry, Impair Autonomous Defenses, covers efforts to disrupt AI-assisted security analysis. For example, hostile content could try to make an automated tool ignore evidence or stop reviewing a file. ATT&CK ID Technique / Sub-Technique Type Description T1697 Steal Application Specific Passwords Technique Attackers phish, generate, or steal application-specific passwords to access accounts without completing the usual MFA checks. T1696 Anti-Automation Evasion Technique Attackers bypass checks designed to block bots, allowing automated activity to continue. T1696.001 Automate CAPTCHA Completion Sub-technique Attackers use automated tools or CAPTCHA-solving services to complete challenges intended to verify human users. T1696.002 Avoid CAPTCHA Sub-technique Attackers avoid triggering CAPTCHA challenges rather than solving them after they appear. T1699 Direct Prompt Injection Technique Attackers submit malicious instructions directly to an AI system’s interface to influence its behavior. T1698 Indirect Prompt Injection Technique Attackers place malicious instructions in outside content that an AI system processes, such as documents or web pages. T1700 AI-Enabled Exfiltration Technique Attackers direct enterprise AI agents to send sensitive information outside the organization. T1608.007 Stage Capabilities: AI Result Poisoning Sub-technique Attackers manipulate web content to influence the information, links, or recommendations returned by AI search tools and assistants. For security teams, the changes offer a clearer way to map activity they already see across business networks, AI tools, phones, and industrial systems. MITRE’s release notes list the additions, and its detailed changelog records what changed from v19.2.

ATT&CK is a knowledge base that helps defenders describe and compare attacker behavior. A technique is a way an attacker may try to achieve a goal, while a detection strategy connects that behavior to data defenders can collect and review.

The framework does not confirm that a specific organization has been breached. Instead, it gives teams a shared language for threat reports, security testing, and detection planning.

items.summary: In about a year, The Gentlemen went from a Qilin affiliate crew in a $48,000 payment dispute to one of the two most active ransomware operations in the world. Its edge isn't novel malware. It's packaging: a centrally maintained pool of an estimated 14,700 pre-compromised FortiGate devices handed to affiliates as a service, an EDR-killer suite that the operators maintain themselves, worm-like propagation that tries up to 21 remote execution paths per host, and a 90/10 revenue split designed to recruit affiliates. Kevin Holvoet, Threat Research Center Lead at the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB), joins Sean O'Connor to walk through CCB's new TLP:CLEAR threat actor profile. We'll cover what the May 2026 leak of the group's own backend revealed, and how chain victimization turns one breach into leverage against the next. items.summary: Linus Torvalds has disclosed that Claude Code helped write Linux kernel patches, test programs, review material, and the first draft of a technical write-up under his direction. A folio represents a group of memory pages, and repeated updates force processor cores to compete over shared data. The proposed approach delays reusing removed page-cache memory until an RCU grace period ends. This gives active readers time to finish before another purpose can use that memory. items.title: Critical Adobe Acrobat Flaw Lets Malicious PDFs Trigger One-Click Memory Corruption
items.summary: Adobe has fixed a flaw in Acrobat and Acrobat Reader that lets a malicious PDF corrupt memory when a user opens it. Tracked as CVE-2026-81983, the out-of-bounds write carries a CVSS score of 7.8 and could lead to code execution with the victim’s user rights. Adobe says it has seen no active exploitation so far. The bug sits in Acrobat’s image pipeline, code that starts parsing image data as soon as a PDF opens. Researchers found it with a custom Python fuzzer built largely with help from a large language model. Instead of randomly modifying full PDF files, the tool created small, valid documents. It changed image fields such as width, height, bit depth, color space, filters, and sample bytes. The strongest crash came from a crafted 16-bit image inside a PDF only 745 bytes in size. The root cause is a 32-bit integer overflow in Acrobat.dll. Acrobat calculates the number of image samples by multiplying an image’s width by its color component count. A second size check adds two bytes for every 16-bit sample. With a very large width, this later value wraps to a tiny number, so Acrobat accepts a very short data stream. Adobe Acrobat Flaw The byte-swap loop still sees a huge sample count and keeps reading and writing past the end of a 16-byte buffer. This causes memory corruption and may give an attacker a path to run code. A proof-of-concept image used a width of 536,870,912, a height of one, 16 bits per component, and the DeviceCMYK color space. Four CMYK components produced a sample count of 0x80000000. The size check approves a buffer the loop then overruns (source : remedio ) According to Remedio research , the related byte-size calculation reached 0x100000000 and wrapped to zero in 32-bit math, allowing an eight-byte stream to pass validation. Opening the PDF was enough to reach the faulty image-rendering path. The CVSS vector shows a local attack path, low attack complexity, no privileges, and required user interaction. A successful exploit can have high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. In practice, attackers still need to deliver the malicious document via email, chat, downloads, or another route. Adobe fixed the issue by using 64-bit math to calculate the sample count and rejecting values above INT_MAX before touching memory. The fix arrived in security bulletin APSB26-141 on September 8, 2026. Adobe patched Acrobat and Reader Continuous 26.002.21900 and earlier with version 26.002.21901. Acrobat 2024 Classic 24.001.30383 and earlier was updated to 24.001.30429. Users and administrators should install the fixed releases without delay, keep automatic updates enabled, and treat unexpected PDF attachments with care. Security teams should also filter suspicious PDFs at email gateways and watch for crashes tied to Acrobat.dll. Adobe lists CVE-2026-81983 as critical, while the NVD record confirms that exploitation needs a victim to open a crafted file. The finding also shows how focused, AI-assisted fuzzing can find deep bugs in old file parsers. items.title: PoC Exploit Released for Critical GitLab RCE Vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229)
items.summary: A public proof-of-concept (PoC) for CVE-2026-97229 published by researcher Jonah Burgess shows how a flaw in GitLab’s CI/CD regular-expression compiler could be used to run commands on a vulnerable server. GitLab rates the issue Critical with a CVSS score of 10.0. The exploit code is publicly available, raising the risk for organizations that have not yet installed the security updates. The PoC targets GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition. Its author reports testing the included exploit layout against the official Linux amd64 GitLab CE 19.4.1 image. The code uses GitLab’s CI lint endpoint, which checks CI/CD configuration files, as part of the exploit chain. The exploit has an important access condition. The attacker needs permission to push a branch to a public project on the affected GitLab instance. The PoC then sends a later request to the CI lint endpoint without a token, cookie, or other authorization header. Jonah Burgess says the command runs as GitLab’s git account, not as an administrator. The public code is an initial release, and its author says further analysis of affected configurations and other possible paths is ongoing. PoC Exploit Released for Critical GitLab Vulnerability GitLab’s advisory describes CVE-2026-97229 as an integer overflow in the CI/CD regular-expression compiler . The PoC details a chain in which CI lint reads a crafted pipeline configuration from an attacker-controlled branch and processes a regular expression against specially named repository paths. A Unicode path causes Ruby to compile the expression again after GitLab’s size check. The exploit authors say this leads to an integer overflow that redirects the regular-expression engine’s execution and reaches a command-execution function. The repository reports that the test request usually ends with an HTTP 502 error because the worker process crashes after the command runs. That response alone does not confirm successful exploitation. Jonah Burgess author’s tests , command output returned through a callback indicated execution. The PoC also requires substantial memory, and the published layout is specific to one GitLab build. The author warns that low memory or multiple concurrent requests could instead disrupt service. GitLab says the flaw affects CE and EE versions 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2. The company released those fixed versions on October 12, 2026, and strongly recommends that self-managed installations upgrade promptly. GitLab.com is already running a patched version, while GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action. Administrators should confirm their version and upgrade to the fixed release for their branch or a later supported version. They should also review recent changes to CI/CD configuration files, especially new or modified regular expressions and project branches. GitLab’s earlier CI/CD regex security coverage and previous security-update reporting provide additional context on why these pipeline components deserve close review. This PoC does not establish that the vulnerability is being used in real-world intrusions. However, it gives defenders a concrete reason to prioritize patching: the issue has the highest CVSS rating, and public exploit code describes a path from project write access to command execution on a vulnerable server. items.title: Critical Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Attackers Escape Virtual Machines and Take Control of Hosts
items.summary: A critical flaw in the Linux kernel may allow an attacker-controlled virtual machine (VM) to breach its isolation boundary and impact the host system. This vulnerability, identified as CVE-2026-99999 and referred to as PwnEscape by researcher Paulos Yibelo, originates from the Linux networking code rather than a specific hypervisor. Paulos Yibelo demonstrated a technique that exposes host memory and, in their lab, progressed to host-level code execution. The flaw is serious for cloud providers and organizations that run untrusted workloads in virtual machines. VM isolation is meant to stop code inside one guest from reaching the host and other workloads. PwnEscape shows how a weakness in a host’s packet-processing path can threaten that boundary, even when the underlying issue is not in the hypervisor itself. PwnEscape Kernel Vulnerability Linux can delay calculating a network packet’s checksum. This is a normal performance feature: packet metadata tells the kernel where the checksum operation should begin and where the result should be written. According to Paulos Yibelo’s PwnEscape report , the problem occurred when less-trusted packet metadata could influence a later write into an IPv4 header. Linux had already processed the packet using the header’s earlier contents. But before fragmentation, the deferred checksum operation could change those contents. Later code then relied on the updated IPv4 header length. In Paulos Yibelo’s test case, the packet initially appeared to have a standard 20-byte IPv4 header. After the deferred write, the header could be interpreted as 60 bytes long. The fragmentation code could then treat bytes beyond the packet’s valid linear data as part of the header and include them in an outgoing packet. He reported that this exposed 32 bytes of host memory. That disclosure is not the same as code execution. The report describes a separate, controlled lab chain in which researchers used host-memory observations and carefully managed allocation behavior to demonstrate selected kernel-memory writes and run a host-root helper. They say this result was reproduced on researcher-owned systems, not as proof of root execution in a cloud provider’s production environment. The distinction matters for readers assessing the risk. A host-memory leak can reveal information that should remain outside a guest’s reach. Further steps may be needed to turn that primitive into control of the host, and the report does not establish that every Linux VM or hypervisor is equally vulnerable. It also notes that stronger validation at packet input needs more work.
